hook.line: Tomás has a café that was his grandmother's, and friends who knew her better than he did. To say any of that, he needs "my", "your" and "her".
hook.es: Mi abuela es de Bogotá, pero mis amigos son de Toronto.
hook.en: My grandmother is from Bogotá, but my friends are from Toronto.

examples.en: Your Spanish is very good (to a friend).
Don Hernando drinks his black coffee.
Do your friends speak English (to a friend)?
Madam, how do you spell your surname (formal)?

rule:
Before a thing, Spanish says whose it is with a short word:

*mi* = my
*tu* = your (to a friend)
*su* = his, her, its, their, or your (formal)

If there's more than one thing, add an -s: *mis amigos*, *tus amigos*, *sus amigos*.

The -s follows the things, not the owner. One grandmother of yours is *tu abuela*; your many friends are *tus amigos*.

*Su* does a lot of work. *Su tinto* can be his, hers, theirs or yours (formal). The conversation tells you which.

Watch the accents: *tu* (your) has none; *tú* (you) has one.

options: Your café is excellent (to a friend).
Vale eats your arepa (to a friend).
Your grandmother is from Bogotá (to a friend).
Is it your coffee (to a friend)?

yourTurn.prompt: Choose *mi* or *mis*: ___ amigos son de Cali.
Say: Your Spanish is very good (to a friend).
yourTurn.why: To a friend, your = *tu*, with no accent.

yourTurn.prompt: Say: Don Hernando drinks his black coffee.
Ask a woman you don't know (formal): Is it your coffee?
Make it plural: Mi cliente es de Medellín.

pitfalls.why: The -s follows the things: several friends, so *mis*.
*Tú* with an accent means you. Your is *tu*, no accent.

pitfalls.wrong: Tomás y Vale trabajan en sus café.
pitfalls.right: Tomás y Vale trabajan en su café.
pitfalls.why: Two people, but one café, so *su*. The -s follows the things, not the owners.

personal: Write three lines about people and things that are yours: your name, your neighbourhood, your friends. Use *mi* or *mis* each time.
